newsitem.title: USA: Somatogen shares bleed on Lilly withdrawal.
newsitem.headline: Somatogen shares bleed on Lilly withdrawal.

text.p: Shares of Somatogen Inc were slammed Thursday on news that Eli Lilly and Co had ended its support of its Optro blood substitute product, raising doubts about the viability of the product.
Analysts said that the news was a setback for the company, as well as for the blood substitute industry.
"This is definitely bad news," said David Crossen, an analyst with Montgomery Securities. "Lilly's action suggests that it does not believe that Optro is a viable product."
On Thursday, Somatogen said that Eli Lilly and Co had decided to discontinue support for the blood substitution product, also known as rHb1.1, under their current collaborative agreement.

"This is negative news for the company and a negaative for the blood substitute industry," said one biotechnology analyst, who declined to be identified. Somatogen shares traded off 3-5/8 to 5-5/8 in late afternoon trade.
Under their agreement, Somatogen and Lilly were collaborating on two studies of the compound, a cardiopulmonary bypass study and an intraoperative study.

"We made the overall assessment of the opportunities to Lilly of the current clincial programs, compared with our other initiatives. We decided to focus on other opportunities," Jim Kappel, a spokesman for Lilly, told Reuters.

Somatogen said it would proceed with the cardiopulmonary bypass study but discontinue the intraoperative study, which deals with elective surgery, such as orthopedic joint replacement. "We are going to be proceeding with the cardiopulmonary study," said Andre de Bruin, chief executive officer, in a telephone interview.
"That is the study that has the fastest path to clinical development and regulatory approval," he said. "As soon as the paperwork is done, we will start enrolling patients."
Stocks of other companies with blood substitute compounds were also hurt Thursday, though not as much as Somatogen.
"There is some reflection of caution out there, but the main culprit is Somatogen," Crossen said.
Northfield Laboratories Inc traded down 3/4 to 10.

Baxter International Inc dropped 1/2 to 45-3/4. Analysts, however, said they felt that whether Baxter's blood product succeeded or failed would not have much impact on the company, which had sales of $5.4 billion in 1996.
Despite the damage to Somatogen's shares, Jim McCamant, editor of the Medical Technology Stock Letter in Berkeley, California, was upbeat.
He said Somatogen has been able to learn from Lilly, including picking up Lilly's production expertise. "This may be a really good thing for Somatogen," he said.
"They could come out of this very strong," said McCamant, who owns Somatogen stock and recommends it in his newsletter's model portfolio.
He agreed with management that the cardiopulmonary application for Somatogen's blood substitutes is the most promising application.

McCamant said one of the benefical effects of a hemoglobin based blood substitute like Optro is that it carries oxygen more effectively than red blood cells do. "Red blood cells get beat up by the artificial heart and lung machinery that they use to oxygenate it," he said.
Crossen was more skeptical. "I'm not optimistic about the potential of Optro in bypass surgery," he said.
